blocks.text: This is a high-yield practical OSCE section. The examiner is usually assessing whether you can perform a procedure safely, aseptically, calmly and correctly, while communicating appropriately with the child/parent.
Explain → Prepare → Check → Asepsis → Perform → Monitor → Dispose → Document

subsections.subsection_title: GENERAL APPROACH TO ANY PEDIATRIC PROCEDURE

subsections.subsection_title: WHAT TO DO IF THE CHILD REFUSES

blocks.text: This is a favourite communication question.

items: “The child refuses the procedure. What do you do?”

blocks.text: “I would first determine why the child is refusing, acknowledge their fear, explain the procedure in age-appropriate language and use appropriate distraction or comfort measures. I would involve the parent and, where possible, give the child appropriate choices. If the procedure is urgent and clinically necessary, I would follow the appropriate consent and safeguarding framework and seek senior assistance rather than simply forcing the procedure.”

“I would explore the parent's concerns, explain the indication, benefits, risks and alternatives in understandable language, and address misconceptions. If the procedure is necessary but the parent continues to refuse, I would seek senior and appropriate legal/ethical advice, particularly if refusal places the child at significant risk.”
“A peripheral IV cannula was inserted successfully on the first attempt into a suitable peripheral vein. Patency was confirmed and the cannula was secured without immediate complication.”

“Peripheral IV access was unsuccessful after an appropriate attempt. I would avoid repeated traumatic attempts and escalate to a more experienced clinician or consider alternative access depending on the child's clinical condition.”
“CSF was not obtained. I would stop further attempts, reassess the indication and contraindications and seek senior assistance.”

“The cannula site is swollen and the infusion is no longer flowing normally, raising concern for infiltration or extravasation. I would stop the infusion immediately and follow the specific extravasation protocol.”
“The child developed coughing and respiratory distress during NG insertion. I would stop advancing the tube, assess the airway and breathing and reassess tube placement before proceeding.”

content_groups.group_title: Q1. What is the most important thing before any invasive procedure?

blocks.text: “Confirm the indication, patient identity, consent, relevant contraindications and prepare appropriate equipment while maintaining asepsis.”

content_groups.group_title: Q2. Why is pain control important in children?

blocks.text: “Children experience pain and distress during procedures, and untreated procedural pain can have immediate and longer-term adverse effects. Appropriate analgesia and non-pharmacological measures improve comfort and cooperation.”

content_groups.group_title: Q3. How do you minimise infection?

blocks.text: “Hand hygiene, appropriate PPE, aseptic technique, sterile equipment where required, skin antisepsis and safe disposal of sharps.”

content_groups.group_title: Q4. What should you do after a needlestick injury?

blocks.text: “Immediately wash the area with soap and water, report the incident promptly and follow the institutional occupational exposure protocol for risk assessment, testing and post-exposure management.”

content_groups.group_title: Q5. How many attempts should you make at venepuncture?

blocks.text: There is no universal number applicable to every situation.

“I would avoid repeated traumatic attempts. After an appropriate unsuccessful attempt, particularly in a distressed child or difficult-access patient, I would reassess and seek assistance according to local policy.”

content_groups.group_title: Q6. Why should you not force a procedure?

blocks.text: “Force can cause injury, increase psychological trauma and reduce future cooperation. Procedures should be performed using appropriate analgesia, restraint only when necessary and proportionate, and experienced assistance.”

For paediatric procedures, technical skill alone is not enough.
The examiner is watching whether you:
Protect the child → prevent pain → prevent infection → perform correctly → recognise complications → communicate professionally.
A candidate who performs a technically correct procedure but forgets consent, analgesia, asepsis, specimen labelling or post-procedure monitoring can still lose substantial marks.
